title: Socially constructed or physiologically informed? Placing humans at the core of understanding cooling needs

findings.quote: "Black Bedouin robes gain two to three times as much heat by radiation from the Sun as white robes, but enhanced convection of air beneath the robe carries this heat away before it reaches the skin"
people shift their sleeping and working habits to avoid heat stress.

findings.antecedent: Entanglements of society, culture, materiality, and human senses
findings.quote: These fields show how cooling needs can be informed by entanglements of society and culture, materiality, and the human senses.

findings.antecedent: Political agenda of 'modernity' and building industries/technology producers
findings.consequent: Social construction of 'comfort' and need for cooling
findings.quote: the social construction of 'comfort' and the need for cooling has been charged by a political agenda of 'modernity' and materially executed by building industries and technology producers with capital interests.

findings.antecedent: Cultural ideology of comfort created by technicians and media
findings.quote: the expansion of AC use was the result of a cultural ideology of comfort created by technicians [10], and media [11]
advertising [12] influenced consumer's preferences towards space conditioning [13].

findings.antecedent: Social practices, habits, ephemeral ideas of hygiene/cleanliness, social etiquettes/conventions
findings.quote: cooling is the result of social practices and habits entrenched in ephemeral ideas of hygiene and cleanliness [14,15] and social etiquettes and conventions [16].

findings.antecedent: Personal history, sensory experience, cultural ideology, policies, new technologies, adaptive thermal strategies
findings.quote: physiological sensations can be shaped by personal history and sensory experience which is both collectively patterned by cultural ideology [20] and policies [21], as well as reshaped by new technologies and everyday adaptive thermal strategies [21].
even a 'view from the window' can alter thermal comfort [23].

findings.antecedent: Preferences and high expectations for thermal satisfaction
findings.quote: preferences and high expectations for thermal satisfaction may hinder the decarbonisation plans in Europe.

findings.consequent: Perception of heat/cold and ambient temperature preferences
findings.quote: women and men perceive heat and cold differently in the built environment, and this informs ambient temperature preferences.
people with an increased Body Mass Index (BMI) are more likely to feel discomfort in warmer ambient environments
people with lower BMI are more likely to feel cold discomfort.

findings.antecedent: Body composition, body fat, skin thickness
findings.consequent: Differentiated reaction of the body to external temperatures, humidity, and air velocity
findings.quote: Body composition, body fat [44] and skin thickness is also responsible for the differentiated reaction of the body to external temperatures, humidity and air velocity [8].

findings.consequent: Preference for higher temperatures (due to lesser body fat/insulation)
findings.quote: People with lower BMI tend to prefer higher temperatures because "of the lesser body fat resulting in lesser insulation" [44] (p. 287).

findings.consequent: Preference for warmer temperatures (due to reduced metabolism and ongoing decline of brain functions)
findings.quote: older people prefer warmer temperatures both as a result of reduced metabolism [49], as well as for those with ongoing decline of brain functions (e.g. dementia) [50]
people who tend to have a lower metabolism (often being women, older people and people affected by obesity or other physical conditions) tend to prefer warmer indoor temperatures [45].

findings.antecedent: Social constructions of gender roles and everyday responsibilities
findings.quote: understanding the social constructions of gender roles and everyday responsibilities can provide insight on how habitus can influence thermal comfort rather than biological differences per se.
Metabolism also changes with social practices, routinised activities and sport.

findings.consequent: Coping with extreme heat (by enhancing thermal transpiration and inducing hypothermia)
findings.quote: thermogenic food such as hot peppers and spicy foods may help people coping with extreme heat because it is believed to enhance thermal transpiration and induce hypothermia.
vigorous exercise imposes significant thermoregulatory stress which may be compounded by the thermal environment

findings.antecedent: Repetitive exposure to high temperatures (e.g., in occupations like miners and builders)
findings.quote: there is a level of adaptation to extreme temperatures that comes through repetitive exposure for a certain period of time, and the body adapts with thermal imprinting (also known as thermal adaptation)

findings.consequent: Ability to adjust to changing temperatures
findings.quote: people exposed to conditioned temperatures (such as air-conditioning) are less able to adjust to changing temperatures than people who prefer natural ventilation

findings.antecedent: Long-term AC use or growing up with AC (thermal history)
findings.consequent: Preference for space conditioning and lower tolerance to warmer temperatures
findings.quote: people exposed to air conditioning for longer hours, or people who grew up with conditioned temperatures (thermal history) tend to prefer space conditioning [70] as they developed a lower tolerance to warmer temperatures.

findings.consequent: Human actions, behaviors, thermoception, and cooling needs
findings.quote: objects (such as the AC) reshape thermoception and create new needs for new cooling comforts [35,72].
the warmth or cold we perceive depend, at least in part, on the different social and material relations we have actualized in order to heat up or cool down.
non-humans' needs (e.g., plants need water, pets need food and thermal comfort) entangle with people's practices, modifying energy decisions.

findings.consequent: Bodily sensations and bodily temperature changes
findings.quote: 'Emotions are felt in the body' claim Nummenmaa et al. [76] who attempt to map the changes reported by the participants who experienced stress, happiness, anxiety, excitement and fear to the body, and bodily temperature.
bodily temperatures can inform or interfere with our emotional states, changing the way we think and behave [78].
temperature (in warm environments) can increase a sense of belonging to a place or a group (affiliation) and affirmation
a cold environment (and physical coldness) can trigger feelings of loneliness
physical warmth (through warm baths) can help reduce the sense of loneliness [79].

findings.consequent: Mind, emotions, memories, and psychological wellbeing
findings.quote: The body informs the mind [80]; what we experience physically, informs emotions, memories and psychological wellbeing - and vice versa.

findings.consequent: Body's internal state (hunger, thirst, hot, cold) and intensity of immediate thermal pleasure
findings.quote: participants were exposed to different sensorial stimuli related to the mechanical creation of thermal comfort (such as air-movement [83], touch [81] and space in the built environment [84]) to find a relationship between the body's internal state (e.g. hunger, thirst, hot, cold) and the intensity of immediate thermal pleasure experienced [85].

findings.antecedent: Prolonged exposure to external stimuli (physical and psychological)
findings.quote: the 'body' is capable of retaining the memory of prolonged exposure to external stimuli at a physical and psychological level [86,87].

findings.antecedent: Lower tolerance to warmer temperatures (due to long-term AC use)
findings.quote: the consumption of space conditioning by those who have developed lower tolerance to warmer temperatures as a result of long-term AC use can been considered addictive [72].
some temperatures may induce certain emotions
emotions or psychological states can regulate body temperatures [89].

findings.consequent: Hyperthermia and change in perceived thermal comfort
findings.quote: emotional stress can be responsible for hyperthermia and therefore a change in perceived thermal comfort [90].
'emotions play a homeostatic role [...]the effects of particular emotional stimuli depend not only on physical temperatures per se but on homeostasis/thermoregulation' (p. 302) [92].
negative emotions alter the sense of thermal comfort.
bodily temperatures evoked by emotions also shape consumption patterns [91,94].

findings.consequent: Thermogenic emotions and people's choices (especially with positive linkages)
findings.quote: memories trigger thermogenic emotions, but they also shape people's choices, especially when there are positively linkages.

findings.consequent: Consumption for certain goods and services (by reinforcing positive neural connections)
findings.quote: nostalgia drives the consumption for certain goods and services as it reinforces positive neural connections [95,96].
long exposure to certain temperatures reshape temperature tolerance levels.

findings.consequent: Memories of how it feels at specific temperatures and environments
findings.quote: the body creates memories of how it feels at specific temperatures and environments, which is meaningful for understanding resulting cooling behaviours.

findings.antecedent: Shape, color, smell, texture, and sound of a space
findings.quote: the shape, colour, smell, texture and sound of a space inform thermal comfort beyond temperature and heat-exchange [74].

findings.antecedent: Characteristics and aesthetics of the material world (colors, light intensity)
findings.consequent: Mind-associations with cold/heat and psychological states
findings.quote: the characteristics and aesthetics of the material world (colours, light intensity and so on) stimulate our mind-associations with cold/heat [107] and psychological states can be triggered by the space, materials and design [113,93].
'Red, for example, is often regarded as a hot color. It is hot not just because it reminds us of blood or fire but also because it arouses our senses.' [108](p. 12).
Lighting intensity and direction, for example, are known for affecting perceived [3] and even illusory temperatures.

findings.consequent: Thermal comfort (for cold environments) and energy consumption
findings.quote: warmer reddish lighting improves people's thermal comfort (for cold environments) without increasing energy consumption.
the colour of one room from a 'warmer' to 'cold' colour such as blue or green, can result in a perceived reduction of the temperature [116,117].
cooler temperatures (e.g., cold white light) might induce a sense of productivity
warmer lights stimulate relaxation [119,120].

findings.consequent: Non-visual impacts and core body temperature
findings.quote: the type and intensity of lighting can trigger non-visual impacts and the exposure time to certain lighting can reduce the core body temperature [121].
furniture materials and space arrangement may stimulate sensorial wellbeing, as well as stimulate or reduce social interactions [122].
thermoception can be informed by different stimuli and interpreted through multiple senses.
acoustic comfort can happen with thermal neutral conditions

findings.antecedent: Decrease in noise level at 500 lx
findings.quote: thermal comfort increases with a "decrease in the noise level at 500 lx" [123] (p. 623).

findings.antecedent: Environment with a window overlooking green areas
findings.quote: people exposed in an environment with a window overlooking green areas felt cooler than the ones without the outside view, despite the thermometer registering the same room temperature for both [22].

findings.antecedent: Ondol (Korean traditional house) with thermal contrasts ('warm floor' and 'cool indoor air')
findings.consequent: Imprinted in people's memory and entangled with gendered practices
findings.quote: the ondol (Korean traditional house) with its thermal contrasts of 'warm floor' and 'cool indoor air' was imprinted in people's memory and entangled with gendered practices

findings.antecedent: External elements (via senses) and mind (assigning meanings)
findings.consequent: Human embodiment and meanings to living spaces/built environment
findings.quote: Humans embody external elements through the senses [126], and the mind assigns meanings to living spaces and the built environment

findings.consequent: Symbolic meanings of status and social power
findings.quote: Through objects people create symbolic meanings of status and social power
Wilhite shows how air conditioning technology is intrinsically linked to social meanings and practices [46]

the flow of knowledge forms an important avenue of socio-cultural influence. Such knowledge can be expert-based... In other cases, industry often promotes expertise on cooling... Orr [130] and Bartel [131] refer to vernacular knowledge as the knowledge people have of their places, which informs indigenous ways to build living spaces [104,132,133] and influences thermal comfort behaviours [131,134].

findings.antecedent: 'Pandiri' (a four-pillared verandah with fresh green leaves)
findings.quote: 'Pandiri' (a four pillared verandah) with fresh green leaves 'provides thermal relief in summer.'

findings.antecedent: Cultural adjustments (siestas, changing dress codes) and 'wet flannel cloths'
findings.quote: Other strategies include cultural adjustments or a change of commonly accepted routines such as taking siestas or changing dress codes. For example, 'wet flannel cloths' are used in the Australian summer [135] to mediate heat

findings.antecedent: Placing a clay pot with water in the corner of the room or increasing room ventilation
findings.quote: placing a clay pot with water in the corner of the room in India [137,138] or increasing room ventilation before using the AC as seen in Japan [16].

findings.antecedent: Vernacular knowledge and modern cooling technologies
findings.consequent: Cooling methods in remote Amazonian communities
findings.quote: in remote Amazonian communities, vernacular knowledge on buildings and cooling methods is often used alongside more modern cooling technologies (e.g. second hand ACs; electric fans).

findings.antecedent: Networks of people (engineers, economists, designers) with industry rhetoric, quantitative models, and performance standards
findings.quote: engineers, economists, and designers, with industry rhetoric, quantitative models and performance standards: "Engineers knew that they largely controlled the air-conditioned environment under a system of custom design."

findings.antecedent: Futuristic models of houses (standards, materials, designs) advanced by architects
findings.consequent: Vulnerability to heat/cold and standardized indoor-climate conditioning
findings.quote: futuristic models of houses "would be more vulnerable to heat and cold [..] and indoor-climate conditioning would become standardized" (p. 17).

findings.antecedent: Social hierarchy, valued norms, and peer influence
findings.consequent: People mirroring each other's behavior, group integration, and identification
findings.quote: People often mirror each other's behaviour, especially in cases of social hierarchy or when there are valued norms promoted by leaders and role models (e.g., priests, political and community leaders). Peer influence is an equally important aspect of the relational sphere, and studies show how people tend towards group integration and identifi-cation [140].

findings.antecedent: AC reliability and credibility transmitted by neighbors
findings.quote: an understanding of AC reliability and credibility transmitted by neighbours had an influence on furthering technological adoption [141] (p. 125).
Whyte [142] observed that word-of mouth may work even better than mass market advertising for air- conditioning in the US.

findings.antecedent: Individuals mirroring others (Lacanian interpretation of desire)
findings.quote: individuals mirror others to create their sense of identity [143].

findings.antecedent: Five-star review mechanism on online platforms
findings.quote: even the five star-review mechanism on online platforms, such as Amazon, provide significant influence for a person's final decision to purchase a specific product [144].

findings.antecedent: Societal rejection of bodily fluids, smells, and odours
findings.quote: the search for acclimatised environments can be linked to societal rejection of bodily fluids [145], smells [146] and odours enhanced by sweating [127].

findings.consequent: Social symboliser of class (e.g., absence of sweat = higher status in Western societies)
findings.quote: sweating and body odours have also been argued to be a social symboliser of class.

findings.consequent: New culture-clothing (e.g., Western business suit) in Asia and removal of logic for traditional dress
findings.quote: the AC has also had a profound transformative effect on the clothes of Asia. Across the region the history of clothing is one deeply rooted in local climatic conditions. The AC not only removed the logic for such forms of dress, but also facilitated the introduction of new forms of clothing, most notably the Western business suit.

findings.consequent: Increasing 'encasement' of people and preferences for indoor environments
findings.quote: air-conditioning is intertwined with the increasing 'encasement' of people and their preferences for indoor environments [35,151,152].

findings.antecedent: Language and vocabulary on thermal sensations
findings.consequent: How people make sense of the world and describe thermal phenomena
findings.quote: The way language and the vocabulary on thermal sensations is constructed in different geographies can have an influence on the way people make sense of the world and describe thermal phenomena [153].

emerging literature on thermal comfort shows the importance of verbal expressions and language differences (e.g. frequent use of adjectives to describe sensations) in reference to measuring personal thermal sensations [154].
Media influence (advertisements, films and videos [155]) on cooling consumer behaviour has been tackled by a few studies [13,141,156].

findings.antecedent: Media messaging (invoking emotions like fears/threats of climate change, culture, perceptions)
findings.quote: Media messaging influences cooling behavioural change by invoking emotions such as fears and perceived threats (e.g., of climate change) [54,55]; culture (patterns of socially shared beliefs, local norms or the lack of; identity, personal standards, valued goals; or contradictions) [59,60]; and perceptions (experience with natural hazards; risk perception) [61].

findings.consequent: Social conditioning of consumption and spreading ideas of modernity/desirability
findings.quote: The role of socio-communication channels such as the TV and social media are central to the underlying social conditioning of consumption and spreading ideas of modernity and desirability. Fatanti et al. [157] showed how popular social media services can influence purchases and travel destinations.
